column1: What are the three systems in the voice's biological signal chain, in order?
column2: Power (breath: diaphragm + intercostals/abdominals) → Oscillator (larynx: vocal folds + intrinsic muscles) → Filter (vocal tract: pharynx, mouth, nose, articulators).

column1: A singer has a 'tight' or 'thin' tone. Which system is almost always the actual cause, and which is commonly misdiagnosed?
column2: The real cause is usually System 1 (breath support) or System 3 (vocal tract shape/jaw tension). It's commonly misdiagnosed as a 'throat' (System 2) problem, wasting time on resonance or breath fixes instead of the true issue.

column1: What is appoggio, and what is it NOT?
column2: Appoggio ('to lean') is active muscular resistance (via intercostals/abdominals) that brakes the diaphragm's natural spring-back during exhale, producing slow controlled airflow. It is NOT actively pushing air out.

column1: In the Aerodynamic Myoelastic cycle, what two forces cause the vocal folds to snap shut after being blown open?
column2: Elastic recoil of the tissue plus the Bernoulli effect (fast airflow through the narrow glottal gap drops local pressure, sucking the folds back together).

column1: What are the two independent levers a singer uses to control pitch and volume, and which muscles/mechanism govern each?
column2: 1) Subglottal pressure (breath support) controls volume/intensity of fold collision. 2) Vocal fold tension controls pitch: cricothyroid stretches folds thin for higher pitch; thyroarytenoid thickens folds for lower pitch/more weight.

column1: Why does singing louder tend to push pitch sharp by default, and what is the training goal regarding this coupling?
column2: Higher subglottic pressure (for more volume) also stretches the vocal folds, raising pitch. Breath pressure and pitch are coupled by default; trained singing actively decouples them so you can get loud without going sharp.

column1: What are typical subglottal pressure values for comfortable speech versus an operatic fortissimo?
column2: Comfortable speech: ~7–10 cm H₂O. Operatic fortissimo: ~25–35 cm H₂O.

column1: What is the singer's formant, and how is it physically produced?
column2: A clustering of resonances F3–F5 around 2.5–3.5 kHz that lets an unamplified classical voice carry over an orchestra. It's produced by widening the throat space above the larynx while narrowing the space just above the vocal folds — a trainable configuration, not innate.

column1: How do F1 and F2 formants relate to jaw/tongue movement?
column2: F1 tracks jaw/tongue height: dropping the jaw raises F1, closing the mouth lowers F1. F2 tracks tongue front-to-back position: front vowels ('ee','eh') raise F2, back vowels ('oo','oh') lower F2.

column1: What effect does raising vs. lowering larynx height have on vowel tone, and why?
column2: Raising the larynx shortens the vocal tract, raising all formants together → brighter, edgier tone. Lowering the larynx lengthens the tract, dropping all formants → darker, rounder tone.

column1: In the Book Breath drill, what observable sign indicates the singer is breathing incorrectly (too high)?
column2: The chest and shoulders rise during inhale instead of staying motionless, and the book on the stomach fails to rise — indicating shallow, high (clavicular) breathing rather than diaphragmatic breathing.

column1: What does an unsteady, sputtering hiss during a sustained breath-support drill indicate?
column2: That airflow is being leaked or dammed inconsistently, usually due to jaw or throat tension interfering with controlled abdominal/intercostal breath release (appoggio).
